As the middle-low member of the charango family, it has a wide and expressive range, able to present everything from a soft low to a clear middle and upper register. Its ten strings are arranged in groups, which produces a rich harmonic resonance, so that each pluck sets the wooden soundbox vibrating deeply and gives a warm, full sound. Beside the bright cleanness of the traditional guitar, the ronroco is fuller and rounder; beside the sharpness of the mandolin, its tone is softer and more inclusive. The soundbox, made of carved wood, gives the instrument its distinctive South American colour, so that its sound is both naturally raw and finely made.

The ronroco is an Andean chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.321-5, the bass or baritone member of the charango family. Its scale length is about 44 to 50 cm, it has 10 strings in 5 groups, and the body is of carved wood or bent sides, unlike the early charango with its armadillo shell. It was created in 1968 by Gonzalo and Wilson Hermosa, members of Los Kjarkas of Cochabamba, Bolivia, was in common use in the 1980s, and was later promoted by the Argentine musician and composer Gustavo Santaolalla.
朗羅科琴為安地斯弦鳴樂器，H-S編號321.321-5，屬恰朗戈琴家族的低音或上: The ronroco is an Andean chordophone, H-S number 321.321-5, the bass or baritone member of the charango family, with a scale length of 44 to 50 cm. It was created in 1968 by the brothers Gonzalo and Wilson Hermosa, members of the Los Kjarkas group of Cochabamba, Bolivia, became widespread in the 1980s, and in the 1990s and 2000s was promoted by the Argentine musician and composer Gustavo Santaolalla. Its important change is that it is made of carved wood or bent sides, unlike the old charango with its armadillo shell.
